findings.location: Expert: configuring compare() for a scoreboard, lines 1428-1429, and the comparer table row 'threshold', line 1442 (also the build_phase comment at line 1015)
findings.quote: `set_threshold(0)` asks for every field to be compared, which matters for field-macro items.
findings.source: IEEE 1800.2-2020 §16.3.6 ('If set_threshold has not been called since the comparer was constructed or since the last call to flush ..., then get_threshold shall return 1') and §5.3.9.1 a) (compare() calls flush when the active object depth is 0); uvm-core 2020.3.1 src/base/uvm_comparer.svh:612-617 (flush() clears miscompares, check_type, result and recursion state, but not m_threshold)
findings.problem: Under the standard, every top-level compare() flushes the comparer, and a flush puts the threshold back to 1. So a set_threshold(0) made once in build_phase stops applying at the first compare(). It persists only because uvm-core 2020.3.1's flush() leaves m_threshold alone. The lesson presents the setting as portable. The bench is not affected, because its hand-written do_compare does not check the threshold.
findings.fix: After the sentence at line 1429 add: "The standard has the comparer's flush() restore the threshold to 1 (§16.3.6), and every top-level compare() flushes first (§5.3.9.1). So a portable scoreboard calls set_threshold(0) before each compare(); in uvm-core 2020.3.1, flush() keeps the threshold, so setting it once in build_phase is enough there." In the threshold row's last cell, append "(in uvm-core 2020.3.1; per §16.3.6 a flush restores 1)".

findings.location: The mid-test reset virtual sequence, line 457
findings.quote: `kill()` (§14.2.5.11) does the same for one sequence and its children, on its default sequencer.
findings.source: IEEE 1800.2-2020 14.2.5.11 (kill removes 'all current locks, grabs, or requests in the sequence's default sequencer'; it says nothing about children or queued responses); uvm-core 2020.3.1 uvm_sequence_base.svh m_kill() (kills every entry in children_array)
findings.problem: "Does the same" ties two things to the standard clause that it does not say. First, killing the children comes from the uvm-core implementation, and the lesson itself labels it that way at line 511 and in Push Further. Second, after the stop_sequences() quote, "the same" also takes in removing queued responses. Clause 14.2.5.11 covers neither. The lesson's own table at line 1819 lists responses only for stop_sequences(). Flashcard auvm9-7 repeats the claim that the clause covers children.
findings.fix: Replace with: "`kill()` (§14.2.5.11) kills one sequence and removes its locks, grabs and requests from its default sequencer; in uvm-core 2020.3.1 it also kills the sequence's children (`m_kill()`)." In content/flashcards/A-UVM-9_Reset_and_Error_Injection.json, card auvm9-7, change "stops one sequence and its children, removing their requests and locks" to "stops one sequence, removing its requests and locks (in uvm-core 2020.3.1 its children are killed too)".

findings.location: Expert: what kill() and stop_sequences() do, line 1810 and the table row at line 1822
findings.quote: | `do_kill()` | called | called (through `kill_sequence()`, uvm-core) |
findings.source: IEEE 1800.2-2020 14.2.5.12 do_kill ('called whenever a sequence is terminated by using sequence.kill or sequencer.stop_sequences (which effectively calls sequence.kill)'); 14.2.4.4
findings.problem: The table marks do_kill() under stop_sequences() as uvm-core behaviour, but 14.2.5.12 itself says do_kill() is called on stop_sequences(). The standard also says stop_sequences() "effectively calls sequence.kill", and kill drops the automatic objection under 14.2.4.4. So uvm-core's failure to drop a top-level sequence's automatic objection on stop_sequences() goes against what the standard implies. The lesson presents it as plain implementation behaviour and does not say the two disagree, though it does say so for post_body.
findings.fix: Change the do_kill row's stop_sequences cell to "called (§14.2.5.12; through `kill_sequence()` in uvm-core)". After "so the phase can hang" at line 1810, add: "(the standard says `stop_sequences()` effectively calls `kill()`, §14.2.5.12, which would drop it: another place where uvm-core and the standard differ)".

findings.location: Address maps: "Registers wider than the bus" table and the paragraph after it (lines 370-377); also Interview angles (line 1475)
findings.quote: In uvm-core 2020.3.1 the access carrying bits [31:0] is issued first in both cases (by source reading of `uvm_reg_map.svh`). So one `TIMESTAMP.read()` becomes two APB reads, and a wrong endianness swaps the halves.
findings.source: uvm-core 2020.3.1 src/reg/uvm_reg_map.svh perform_accesses lines 1953-1955 and 1994-1996: `if ((rw_access.kind == UVM_WRITE) && (endian == UVM_BIG_ENDIAN)) { >> { rw_access.data }} = { << byte { rw_access.data}};` (and the same for reads after bus2reg). rw_access.data is uvm_reg_data_t, `UVM_REG_DATA_WIDTH = 64 bits by default (uvm_reg_defines.svh). IEEE 1800.2-2020 17.2.2.4 (UVM_BIG_ENDIAN: most-significant bytes first in consecutive addresses)
findings.problem: The paragraph presents the big-endian row as uvm-core behaviour, by source reading, but the same function also reverses the bytes of every big-endian access, and it does so over the whole 64-bit uvm_reg_data_t. On this lesson's 4-byte map the reversed write data lands in bits [63:32], so a 32-bit adapter field gets 0. On a read the bus word is moved into the upper half and then cut off by the n_bytes mask, so the model sees 0. Even where the bus is as wide as the data type, a wrong endianness setting reverses all the bytes, not just the halves. The lesson records other implementation limitations, so leaving this one out of a table described as uvm-core behaviour is a material gap.
findings.fix: After the sentence ending "...by source reading of `uvm_reg_map.svh`)", add: "The same function also byte-reverses each access on a `UVM_BIG_ENDIAN` map, over the whole 64-bit `uvm_reg_data_t`. On a bus narrower than 8 bytes, that moves the data out of the bits a 32-bit adapter copies, so writes send 0 and reads return 0 (uvm-core 2020.3.1, by source reading: check your library version before you rely on big-endian maps)." Change "a wrong endianness swaps the halves" to "a wrong endianness puts the halves at the wrong addresses". Leave the interview prompt as it is, or add "(and, in uvm-core, the byte order within each word)" to its hint.

findings.source: IEEE 1800.2-2020 E.1 (exclusion "matches the full name of the block or register"), E.3.1 and E.5.1 ("writing it through its default address map"), E.4.1 ("making sure the resulting value matches the mirrored value"), E.6.1 ("performed for each map in which the memory is defined"); uvm-core 2020.3.1 uvm_reg_hw_reset_seq.svh (field-level NO_REG_HW_RESET_TEST lookup), uvm_reg_access_seq.svh and uvm_mem_access_seq.svh (foreach maps), uvm_reg_mem_shared_access_seq.svh (exp = rg.get() & ~wo_mask[k]), uvm_mem_walk_seq.svh (continue when get_access(map) != "RW")
findings.problem: The page says the table lists every difference, but at least four used on this page are missing from it: (1) field-level NO_REG_HW_RESET_TEST, which rule 4 and the Make It Work bench rely on, exists only in uvm-core, because E.1 names block or register only; (2) the register access and memory access tests run through every map in uvm-core, but through the default map in E.3.1 and E.5.1; (3) shared access compares with get() in uvm-core, but with the mirrored value in E.4.1 (the same difference the table already lists for bit-bash); (4) the walk skips maps that are not RW in uvm-core, while E.6.1 says each map.

findings.location: Kata, worked solution, 'How to check yourself', line 1326; Debugging table row 2, line 530
findings.quote: In step 2, if bit-bash fails on BOOT bit 1 or 0, the `set_compare()` call came after `start()`; if it fails on a bit above 15, the DUT drives an unused bit.

The hint, and the debug-table advice to compare 'that bit', send the learner to the bit number in the message instead of the bit that differs.

Because bit-bash compares the whole register, one bad bit makes every tested bit's check fail." Debug table row 2, Fix column: start with "XOR the yielded and expected values to find the differing bit (it may differ from bit #k)," and keep the rest.

findings.location: Make It Work, file-map table row tb_top (line 467); 'Run it' paragraph (line 719); Run 1 and Run 3 'Expected output' notes (lines 734, 826)
findings.quote: UVM applies time values passed to it, such as the `set_timeout(1ms)` argument, and prints `@ time`, in that unit. With a 1 ps unit the timeout would fire at 1 µs, before item 57, and the logs below would print times in ps.
findings.source: IEEE 1800-2023 §20.4.3 and Table 20-3 (the default $timeformat units_number is the smallest time precision argument of all `timescale directives); uvm-core 2020.3.1 src/base/uvm_report_server.svh:891 `$swrite(time_str, "%0t", $realtime)`; contradicts I-UVM-1D index.mdx line 712 ('your simulator prints %t in its own units, by default the smallest time precision, IEEE 1800-2023 §20.4.3') and this module's own index.mdx line 674 and hang-lab.mdx line 816, which call $timeformat so that UVM prints ns
findings.problem: uvm-core formats the report time with %0t. With no $timeformat call, %t prints in the smallest time precision in the design, not in uvm_pkg's time unit. This file's `timescale 1ns/1ps sets that precision to 1 ps, so a compliant simulator prints the first failure as `@ 1165000`, not `@ 1165`, even when uvm_pkg is compiled at 1 ns exactly as 'Run it' asks. So the printed logs in Runs 1 to 3 are not what this code prints. The lesson gives the wrong cause (uvm_pkg's unit) in three places, and that contradicts the prerequisite I-UVM-1D and the two sibling lessons in this module. The set_timeout half of the sentence is right (§1.4.5) and must stay.
findings.fix: In tb_top's initial block, insert `$timeformat(-9, 0, "", 0);   // %t prints ns with no suffix, so the logs show "@ 1165:"` before `run_test("add_rand_test");`. The empty suffix keeps the log lines matching the signature script's `@ ?\d+:` pattern. In 'Run it', replace '…and prints `@ time`, in that unit. With a 1 ps unit the timeout would fire at 1 µs, before item 57, and the logs below would print times in ps.' with '…in that unit; with a 1 ps unit the timeout would fire at 1 µs, before item 57. The `@ time` of each log line is printed with `%0t`, whose units are set by `$timeformat` and default to the smallest time precision in the design (IEEE 1800-2023 §20.4.3), here 1 ps; the `$timeformat` call in `tb_top` makes the logs below print ns.' In the tb_top file-map row, replace '(printed in `uvm_pkg`'s time unit; see "Run it")' with '(printed in ns by the `$timeformat` call; see "Run it")'.

findings.location: Make It Work > 'What each piece guarantees', second bullet (line 457) and 'The wrap in numbers' table (lines 464-471)
findings.quote: PSS gives a sum the width of its widest operand (§8.7.1), so a 32-bit `dst + len` can wrap past 0xFFFFFFFF
findings.source: Accellera PSS 3.0 §8.7 and §8.7.1 Table 20 ('Unsized constant number: At least 32'); §8.7 says an expression's size depends on 'the context in which the expression appears'
findings.problem: Table 20 gives the self-determined width of a sum, max(L(i),L(j)). In `dst + len <= 0x80100000`, though, the sum is an operand of a comparison with an unsized hex literal. Table 20 says only that such a literal is 'at least 32' bits, and the PSS table has no row for relational operators. So whether the sum is really evaluated in 32 bits (and so wraps) depends on the tool's literal width. The table states the wrap as certain ('the carry out of bit 31 is lost'). The safe form the model uses is correct either way, so this is a precision note, not an error.
findings.fix: After '(§8.7.1)' add: "and an unsized constant is only 'at least 32' bits (Table 20), so in a tool that evaluates the comparison in 32 bits". In the table's 'Evaluate the arithmetic in 32 bits' row add "(if the tool sizes the comparison at 32 bits)". Leave the conclusion unchanged: bounding `dst` itself is safe whatever width the tool uses.

findings.location: Make It Work > 'What each piece guarantees', second bullet, last sentence (line 457)
findings.quote: The right-hand side `0x80100000 + 0x100000 * chan.instance_id - len` stays above 0x800FF000, so nothing in it wraps.
findings.source: Lesson's own constraints (len in [64..4096], instance_id 0 or 1): the minimum is 0x80100000 - 0x1000 = 0x800FF000 exactly
findings.problem: With channel 0 and len = 4096, the right-hand side equals 0x800FF000. It does not go above it. The conclusion that nothing wraps still holds.
findings.fix: Replace "stays above 0x800FF000" with "is never below 0x800FF000".

findings.location: Build Your Mental Model > How the two sides talk / packing-order table, line 466, and Retrieval quiz Q4 (lines 1406, 1410)

findings.location: Build Your Mental Model > The split, 'The monitor pushes instead of pulling' (line 400); Make It Work, axi_wr_mon_bfm (line 1004)
findings.quote: the BFM holds a handle to its proxy, a **back-pointer**: the proxy writes `bfm.proxy = this;` through its virtual interface ... / axi_wr_monitor proxy;                        // set by the proxy: the back-pointer
findings.source: Lesson's own rules at line 438 ('A class handle ... cannot be an argument to a BFM task that becomes hardware') and line 485 ('Class handles, dynamic arrays, queues and `chandle` arguments on the HDL side are not in the subset'); line 514 and line 671 name only the time-consuming BFM tasks as the vendor extension
findings.problem: The lesson says over and over that class handles cannot exist on the HDL side. Then the HDL-side monitor BFM stores a class handle (`axi_wr_monitor proxy`) and calls a method through it. Nothing tells the learner that this back-pointer is also part of the vendor remote-call style (DVCon US 2011 §4.3.2, already cited) and not standard SCE-MI 2, where the outbound push would be a DPI import or SV-Connect call. A junior meets what looks like a contradiction with no explanation. Line 671 lists only the time-consuming tasks as the vendor-extension part.
findings.fix: After 'and the BFM calls `proxy.burst_seen(b)` at the end of each burst.' insert: 'The back-pointer is a class handle stored in HDL-side code, so it is part of the same vendor remote-call style as the BFM tasks (DVCon US 2011 §4.3.2): the tool treats the call through it as a call to the host and does not build hardware for it. In standard SCE-MI 2 the same push is an outbound DPI import call (SV-Connect, §5.6.3).' In the Make It Work code-style note (line 671), change 'And the BFMs use time-consuming tasks called from the HVL side' to 'And the BFMs use time-consuming tasks called from the HVL side, and the monitor BFM holds a class back-pointer to its proxy'.

findings.location: Lock-step section lead-in, 'What riscv-dv's own compare checks' paragraph, line 513, and the comparison table rows at lines 517 and 520
findings.quote: compares the sequence of **integer-register updates** in two trace CSVs: it skips instructions that write no register, never compares stores directly (a bad store shows up only if a later load reads it back), and counts leftover register-writing entries as mismatches.
findings.source: chipsalliance/riscv-dv master scripts/instr_trace_compare.py (fetched 2026-11-15): check_update_gpr() returns 1 only when rd_val != gpr[rd], or when a first write is nonzero; the in-order loop skips an entry when gpr_state_change_1 == 0; the loop breaks when trace_2_index == len(instr_trace_2); only the instr_trace_2 tail is scanned afterwards ('Check if there's remaining instruction that change architectural state'), and there is no handling for leftover trace-1 entries
findings.problem: The lesson says riscv-dv's compare is stronger than it is, in a passage meant to warn learners what that compare misses. (1) The script compares only register writes that change a register's value. A write of the value the register already holds is skipped, and so is a first write of 0. The lesson says only instructions that write no register are skipped. (2) Leftover entries count as mismatches only in the second trace. Once the second trace runs out, the loop breaks, and any later register-changing entries in the first trace are never checked or counted. The table row 'Leftover register-writing entries count as mismatches' therefore holds in one direction only.
findings.fix: Line 513: replace 'it skips instructions that write no register, never compares stores directly (a bad store shows up only if a later load reads it back), and counts leftover register-writing entries as mismatches.' with 'it skips any instruction that does not change a register's value (no register write, or a write of the value the register already holds), never compares stores directly (a bad store shows up only if a later load reads it back), and counts leftover value-changing entries as mismatches only in the second trace: once the second trace runs out, the rest of the first trace is never checked.' Line 517 cell: 'Only those that change an integer register's value'. Line 520 cell: 'Leftovers in the second trace count as mismatches; leftovers in the first trace are not checked'.

findings.location: Push Further, 'Expert: Lock-step co-simulation in a production UVM bench', line 1058, and the SequenceDiagram 'Ibex's calls for one retirement, in order' at lines 1060-1081
findings.quote: Before each step it calls, in this order: `riscv_cosim_set_debug_req`, `riscv_cosim_set_nmi`, ... then `riscv_cosim_step(rd_addr, rd_wdata, pc, trap, rf_wr_suppress)`. ... Separate threads notify every data-side access and instruction-fetch bus errors.
findings.source: lowRISC/ibex master dv/uvm/core_ibex/common/ibex_cosim_agent/ibex_cosim_scoreboard.sv, run_cosim_rvfi: before set_debug_req, it pops iside_error_queue entries whose order is older than this retirement. findings.problem: The text calls this list the full order, and the diagram is titled 'in order', but both leave out the conditional riscv_cosim_set_iside_error call. findings.fix: Line 1058: insert 'if an instruction-fetch error was queued for this retirement, `riscv_cosim_set_iside_error`;' before `riscv_cosim_set_debug_req`, and change the last sentence to 'A separate thread notifies every data-side access; another thread queues instruction-fetch bus errors, which the per-retirement path forwards with set_iside_error.' In the diagram, add { from: "scb", to: "iss", label: "riscv_cosim_set_iside_error (only if a fetch error is queued for this order)" } as the first message under the 'per retirement' divider.

findings.location: LLMs as drafting tools, catalogue item 8 and the paragraph after it (lines 234-236); Reviewing AI-generated SVA, table row 8 (line 324)
findings.quote: 8. **Invented APIs:** methods, macros, plusargs or system functions that do not exist ... Only item 8 is caught by the compiler, and only if the invented name is not an existing name used wrongly.  /  | 8. Invented APIs | No, unless an existing name is used wrongly | The compiler |
findings.source: IEEE 1800-2023 §21.6: a plusarg name is only a string argument to $test$plusargs/$value$plusargs. If no matching plusarg is given, these functions return 0 at run time; no compile error occurs. Unknown methods, macros and system functions do fail to compile or elaborate.
findings.problem: Item 8 lists invented plusargs ('a plusarg nothing reads', line 223), but the lesson then says the compiler catches item 8. An invented plusarg such as $test$plusargs("FAST_MODE") compiles and quietly returns 0, which makes it one of the silent defects. The table's 'Compiles? No' teaches the opposite.
findings.fix: Line 236: 'Only item 8 is usually caught by the compiler: an unknown method, macro or system function fails to compile, but an invented plusarg is just a string, so `$test$plusargs("...")` compiles and silently returns 0.' Line 324, Compiles? column: 'No for methods, macros and system functions; yes for an invented plusarg'. First check column: 'The compiler (for a plusarg: check that something reads it)'.

findings.location: LLMs as drafting tools, 'Check your list' reveal, finding 5 (line 270)
findings.quote: 5. **Width trap.** If `fifo_count` is declared with `$clog2(MAX_DEPTH)` bits, it cannot represent `MAX_DEPTH`, and `fifo_count <= MAX_DEPTH` can never fail.
findings.source: IEEE 1800-2023 §20.8.1 ($clog2). For a MAX_DEPTH that is not a power of two, for example 5, $clog2(5) = 3 bits holds 0 to 7, so it can represent MAX_DEPTH.
findings.problem: The claim holds only when MAX_DEPTH is a power of two. As written it is stated as a general rule.
findings.fix: 'If `fifo_count` is declared with `$clog2(MAX_DEPTH)` bits and MAX_DEPTH is a power of two (such as 4), it cannot represent `MAX_DEPTH`, and `fifo_count <= MAX_DEPTH` can never fail.'
